summary.label: Rich
summary.headline: Equity valuations sit roughly one standard deviation above long-run averages. The equity risk premium has compressed to ~65 bps as the 10Y trades at 4.31% while earnings yields have fallen. Markets are not in bubble territory but leave little margin for multiple expansion.

metrics.name: S&P 500 Forward P/E
metrics.subtitle: Next 12-month earnings estimate
metrics.label: rich
metrics.interpretation: 1.7 standard deviations above the 35-year mean. Only the 1999 dot-com peak and 2020-21 stimulus era were materially richer. Requires sustained earnings growth to justify.

metrics.name: Earnings Yield
metrics.subtitle: Inverse of forward P/E
metrics.label: rich
metrics.interpretation: Near 35-year lows outside of the tech bubble. Investors are accepting lower earnings compensation for equity risk.

metrics.name: Equity Risk Premium
metrics.subtitle: Earnings yield minus 10Y Treasury
metrics.label: expensive
metrics.interpretation: Compensation for holding stocks over bonds has collapsed. Historically this configuration preceded either rate cuts or equity drawdowns; today it reflects faith in AI-driven earnings acceleration.

metrics.name: Market Cap / GDP
metrics.subtitle: Wilshire 5000 / Nominal GDP (Buffett Indicator)
metrics.label: expensive
metrics.interpretation: Roughly 2.8 standard deviations above the 50-year mean. Even adjusting for structurally higher tech margins and foreign revenue, this is in the most extreme decile of readings.

metrics.name: Shiller CAPE
metrics.subtitle: Cyclically adjusted P/E (10-year real earnings)
metrics.label: expensive
metrics.interpretation: Above every historical reading except 1999 (peak 44). CAPE is a blunt instrument over short horizons but has consistently predicted lower forward 10-year returns when above 30.

metrics.name: S&P 500 Dividend Yield
metrics.subtitle: Trailing 12-month dividends / price
metrics.label: rich
metrics.interpretation: Dividend yields are compressed by buyback-heavy capital return policies and elevated share prices. Less reliable as a valuation signal post-2000, but still directionally informative.

methodology: Each metric is compared to its own historical distribution. A z-score is computed as (current - mean) / stdev. Metrics where higher values imply richer valuations (P/E, CAPE, cap/GDP) are labeled cheap (z < -1), fair (-1 ≤ z < 0), rich (0 ≤ z ≤ 1), or expensive (z > 1). Yield-type metrics where lower values imply richer valuations (earnings yield, ERP, dividend yield) use the inverse sign. The composite score is the mean z-score across all metrics, mapped to 0-10 via a sigmoid.
disclaimer: Valuation signals have historically predicted 10+ year forward returns reasonably well but are poor timing indicators. Expensive markets can remain expensive for years. This is a research tool, not investment advice.
